one_liner: Personal QuickJS-NG fork with inline caches and interpreter fast paths; Octane 2022 to 2385 (+18%) against upstream quickjs-ng on CI.
what_it_does: A fork of quickjs-ng (itself a fork of Bellard's QuickJS), the small embeddable ES2023+ JavaScript engine with a C API, the qjs shell and the qjsc bytecode compiler. Its C API is quickjs-ng 0.17.0 plus additions (TypeScript type erasure via JS_EVAL_FLAG_TYPESCRIPT, async module loading via JS_LoadModuleAsync and friends, JS_SetModuleMetaFunc), so most embedders swap the sources and rebuild. It also ships an npm package @gkurt/quickjs-wasi (0.3.0) and a rquickjs-sys build for Rust.
how_it_is_fast: Shape-keyed inline caches for property reads, writes and adds (two-way, including adds that shadow prototype properties), a 256-entry per-context cache of global variable slots that validates itself on each hit, and dictionary-mode shapes for objects with up to 1024 properties. The interpreter gains fused opcodes (OP_to_propkey_cond for obj[key] = v, OP_to_int32, compare-and-branch fusion), dense-array recovery for arrays that went slow, interrupt polling only on backward jumps and calls, and in-place string appends. Library paths add computed-goto regexp dispatch with memchr skip-ahead (REOP_skip_to_char, REOP_skip_to_range), a native numeric sort when the comparator's bytecode is exactly (a, b) => a - b or b - a, direct-to-buffer JSON.stringify, atom-keyed JSON.parse, and properties allocated inline with the object.
when_to_use: You already embed quickjs-ng and want more interpreter throughput on object-heavy or array-heavy scripts without a JIT (Octane total +18% vs upstream in PR #8, with more gains claimed by PRs #9 and #12 against the fork's own earlier heads).
Scripts dominated by property access on stable object shapes, global variable traffic, numeric sort with a - b comparators, JSON.stringify/parse, or regexp scans with a literal first character.
WASI or Rust (rquickjs) embeddings where you can take the fork's prebuilt npm or rquickjs-sys artefacts and track one maintainer's release tags (v0.17.0-gkurt.N).
Throughput matters more than peak memory or binary size.
when_not_to_use: Memory-constrained targets: PR #8 measured peak memory over full Octane +18% (CodeLoad 60 to 84 MB, PdfJS 18 to 23 MB) and qjs code size +12% versus upstream.

You need a maintained, reviewed engine: the fork is three weeks old (13 PRs, 2026-09-14 to 2026-09-29), has 0 stars, 0 issues, one human maintainer, and its commits are written by an AI assistant on claude/... branches; nothing has been proposed upstream.

You exchange precompiled bytecode or snapshots with stock quickjs-ng: BC_VERSION is 35 in the fork and each side rejects the other's bytecode; @gkurt/quickjs-wasi 0.2.0 snapshots do not restore in 0.3.0.

Your code is written against current quickjs-ng master: upstream changed JSInterruptHandler to take a JSContext *, the fork still passes a JSRuntime *, so it is not a drop-in for the newest upstream API.
Workloads like Gameboy (-5%) or microbench global_write (+50% time) and array_for (+16%), which PR #8 lists as slower than upstream.

integration.dependencies: none (libc and libm; optional mimalloc as upstream)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler, CMake 3.10+ (also Meson and a Makefile wrapper); computed-goto regexp dispatch needs GCC or Clang, not MSVC or Emscripten
integration.platforms: same as quickjs-ng: Linux, macOS, Windows (MSVC, including ARM64 with Visual Studio 18), WASI; 32-bit NaN-boxing builds syntax-checked per PR #9
integration.thread_safety: As upstream: one JSRuntime per thread, no locking; the new caches live in JSContext/JSRuntime and the fork adds no process-wide mutable state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — source-compatible with quickjs-ng 0.17.0 plus extra APIs, but bytecode (BC_VERSION 35) is incompatible and the JSInterruptHandler signature differs from current upstream master

gotchas: Only PR #8 (fork 4679cbc vs quickjs-ng 19dbe85) measures against upstream; PRs #9 and #12 measure the fork against its own previous head, so their +22.1% Octane and -21% runtime.js figures do not multiply with PR #8's +18%. The weekly bench-upstream job keeps running (run #10 on 2026-10-05) but its summary sits behind a GitHub sign-in, so no post-PR #12 fork-vs-upstream number was readable here. The 1.57x runtime.js figure comes from the fork's own micro benchmarks, which bench/README.md says are written to exercise the paths each optimization targets; upstream's tests/microbench.js (1.18x) and Octane (+18%) are the less biased numbers.

Harness read in full (bench-upstream.yml, bench/octane.js, bench/upstream.js, upstream tests/microbench.js): both sides use identical CMake/Makefile flags (diffed against upstream; the fork only adds a QJS_DISABLE_TYPESCRIPT option and test targets), run alternately on one runner, and the cachegrind counts run upstream's calibrated iteration counts on both. No correctness bug found; one small flaw: the Octane total is the geometric mean of each side's successful benchmarks only, so a suite that errors on one side would change the set compared (the report prints such failures, none were reported in PR #8).
Interrupt handlers are polled only on backward jumps and function entry, so long straight-line code is checked less often than upstream.
TypeScript type erasure is compiled in by default (QJS_DISABLE_TYPESCRIPT turns it off), part of the code-size growth.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Bellard's QuickJS or stock quickjs-ng when you want that exact engine and C API but faster, and can accept an unreviewed single-maintainer fork; PrimJS claims a similar Octane gain over QuickJS (3735 vs 2904) from a company-backed codebase, and Escargot or Hermes are better choices if you can switch engines and want a long-maintained one.
verified_claims_summary: On a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest runner (CPU not stated, compiler not named, both sides built with make BUILD_TYPE=Release), medians of 3 alternating runs put the fork at 2385 vs 2022 Octane 2.0 geomean score against upstream quickjs-ng 19dbe85 (+18%), 1.18x faster on upstream's tests/microbench.js and 1.57x on the fork's runtime.js with 35% fewer instructions, at +18% peak memory and +12% code size. Later PRs report further gains against the fork's own earlier heads only.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-09-29, release v0.17.0-gkurt.1, weekly benchmark job still running) and MIT-licensed, but a 0-star, AI-authored personal fork three weeks old with no upstream review, so vendor it only with your own test262 and fuzzing runs.
